analysis.one_liner: Bars federal money from being used to deploy or keep U.S. troops in Iraq.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut off funding for deploying troops in Iraq was never voted on; it sat in two House committees for the rest of the 109th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited any federal funds from being spent to deploy or keep U.S. Armed Forces in Iraq, with exceptions for the money needed to withdraw troops safely and for diplomatic and financial support to Iraq's government and security forces. It would have ended U.S. military participation in the Iraq War by using Congress's power of the purse. Instead, it was referred to the Armed Services and International Relations committees and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. service members and their families would gain most directly: the bill would have removed them from an active war zone except for the troops needed for a safe withdrawal. Taxpayers would also save the cost of continuing combat operations, while Iraqi civilians would lose the presence of foreign troops fighting in their country.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits funds from being obligated or expended to deploy or continue to deploy U.S. Armed Forces to Iraq [S3].
Allows funding for a safe and orderly withdrawal of troops from Iraq, so service members are not left without support during pullout [S3].

Preserves funds for diplomacy with Iraq, foreign governments, NATO, and the UN, and for financial assistance or equipment to Iraqi and international forces, so the transition to Iraqi-led security could continue [S3].
Explicitly permits non-Defense agencies to keep funding social and economic reconstruction in Iraq, so civilian aid was not cut [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the contractors and supply chains built around war operations would lose revenue, and critics warned a funding cutoff could destabilize Iraq before its own forces were ready. The Bush administration and congressional leadership would lose the ability to set war policy through appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: War contractors and the war's supporters

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts off combat funding but still allows money and equipment to flow to Iraqi and international forces, so critics could argue the fighting would continue without U.S. troops able to protect themselves during operations [S3].

Opponents of war-funding cutoffs generally argued that pulling funding abruptly could leave Iraq unstable and undermine the security transition the bill itself allows for; the bill offers no timeline or conditions for Iraqi forces taking over, only a funding prohibition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who bore the war's costs — service members deployed repeatedly, their families, and taxpayers — the benefit of ending deployment was large and direct. The cost, an abrupt transition to Iraqi-led security, was real but the bill tried to soften it by funding withdrawal, diplomacy, and Iraqi forces. As a piece of legislation it was narrow and clear; its weakness was political, not design: it never got a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Armed Services and International Relations committees, neither of which ever brought it up, so it died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McGovern introduced the bill on November 4, 2005, with 12 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the Committee on Armed Services and, in addition, to the Committee on International Relations [S1].
Nineteen Democrats cosponsored the bill in total [S4].
The action history shows no committee markups, no hearings, no floor action, and no vote after the referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The war continued as it was, so the Bush administration kept the war funding and policy it already had, and defense contractors and military suppliers kept the revenue from ongoing operations. Service members continued to deploy instead of coming home.

for.name: Rep. Jim McGovern
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut off funds for deploying troops to Iraq.

for.name: 19 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 12 signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for markup or consideration, so it went nowhere in committee.

against.name: House International Relations Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the second committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats, and Republicans controlled the committees and floor calendar that never acted on it; there is no record of any Republican support [S4].

industries.note: A funding cutoff for deploying troops to Iraq would end the combat operations that defense firms supply — equipment, logistics, and munitions — cutting a major revenue stream. Their continued revenue depends on the war continuing, which runs against troops and taxpayers footing the cost.

industries.industry: Private military and reconstruction contractors in Iraq
industries.note: Combat funding would stop, but the bill explicitly allows continued spending on reconstruction, Iraqi security forces, and withdrawal logistics, so some contracting work would continue. The net effect depends on how much of the work was tied to combat versus these allowed activities.
